title: The Rhyming Poem
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A unique experiment in Old English prosody: an elegiac meditation on the fall of a once-powerful lord, written in rhyming couplets with end-rhyme sustained line after line, a technique otherwise foreign to alliterative verse. The speaker remembers his former glory as a generous ruler surrounded by retainers, and contrasts it with his present misery and loss.
plot_or_argument: The speaker recalls his past prosperity as a lord who distributed treasure and ruled a loyal comitatus, then laments the reversal of fortune that has stripped him of wealth, retainers, and honour. The poem moves from remembered joy to the recognition that all earthly glory decays, and closes with reflection on the grave and the soul's fate.
narrative_structure: A single first-person meditation organized around the contrast between past splendour and present ruin, framed by ubi sunt reflection; the paired rhymes and internal rhymes bind short clauses into couplets.
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed couplets with pervasive end-rhyme and internal rhyme over an alliterative base; the poet sustains rhyme through some 87 lines, a virtuoso performance in a language whose native metre is alliterative.
historical_context: Composed in the later Old English period, when the heroic conventions of the hall and the comitatus were already literary memory rather than living institutions; the poem shares the vocabulary of exile and transience with The Wanderer and The Seafarer.
literary_significance: The earliest extended rhyming poem in English; evidence that Old English poets could adapt the alliterative line to rhyme, anticipating the rhyming experiments of later medieval English verse.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. No attribution has ever been proposed.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 94r-95v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: Resignation
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A first-person penitential prayer in which the speaker, an exile and outcast from his lord's favour, submits himself wholly to God's will and prays for guidance through the storms of life. The poem fuses the secular conventions of the exile's lament with Christian devotion.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, alienated from his earthly lord and wandering in misery, turns to God as his true protector, acknowledging that he has suffered for his sins, and prays for wisdom, steadfastness, and a safe passage through life's sea of troubles to the heavenly home.
narrative_structure: A sustained first-person prayer in which the imagery of exile, sea-voyage, and homelessness is progressively reinterpreted as the soul's spiritual condition; some editors detect a break in the middle of the text suggesting an incomplete or composite poem.
meter_and_prosody: Standard alliterative long line with the formulaic diction of the elegiac tradition; the poem is textually imperfect, with apparent lacunae.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the late Old English religious lyric, where the conventions of heroic exile poetry were appropriated for penitential devotion; comparable to The Wife's Lament in its fusion of personal loss and landscape imagery.
literary_significance: A major example of the Old English religious lyric's absorption of elegiac conventions, and a witness to the penitential spirituality of late Anglo-Saxon England.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The title 'Resignation' is an editorial convenience, not in the manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 117v-119v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Descent into Hell
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A narrative poem on Christ's descent into hell between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection, his release of the patriarchs and prophets, and the Resurrection itself. It draws on the Gospel of Nicodemus tradition and dramatizes the harrowing as a triumphant act of liberation.
plot_or_argument: Christ descends to hell, breaks its gates, and frees the captive righteous — Adam, the patriarchs, and the prophets — who greet him as their long-awaited redeemer. The poem closes with the women's discovery of the empty tomb and the angel's announcement of the Resurrection.
narrative_structure: A compact narrative in two movements: the harrowing itself (the descent, the breaking of the gates, the speeches of the patriarchs) and the Resurrection morning at the tomb, with typological echoes of the Exodus throughout.
principal_characters: Christ, Adam, the patriarchs and prophets, the women at the tomb
literary_form: religious narrative poem in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with formulaic phrasing; the speeches of the patriarchs are given rhetorical weight through balanced alliterative clauses.
historical_context: The harrowing of hell was a central motif of early medieval devotion, represented in art and liturgy as well as poetry; the poem is contemporary with the flourishing of the theme in Anglo-Saxon stone sculpture and homiletic prose.
literary_significance: The only surviving Old English poem devoted wholly to the harrowing of hell, and an important witness to the devotional imagination that also produced The Dream of the Rood and Christ III.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. No attribution has been proposed.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 119v-121v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: Azarias
alternative_titles: The Canticle of the Three Youths
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A poem on the ordeal of the three youths — Azarias, Ananias, and Misael — in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, based on Daniel 3 and on the canticle of praise they sing from the flames. The poem shares a substantial passage with the Junius manuscript poem Daniel.
plot_or_argument: The three youths refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and are cast into the furnace; protected by the angel of God, they walk unharmed amid the flames and sing a canticle of praise in which all creation is summoned to bless the Lord, from the heavens and waters to the beasts and the sons of men.
narrative_structure: A bipartite structure: a brief narrative of the ordeal followed by the long canticle of praise, a liturgical catalogue of creation in the manner of the Benedicite.
literary_form: religious narrative poem with embedded canticle
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the canticle's catalogues of creation are carried by parallel alliterative phrases in the liturgical style.
historical_context: The story of the three youths was read typologically in Anglo-Saxon England: the furnace prefigured both the Incarnation (the fire that does not burn) and the Church's endurance under persecution. The poem is closely related to Daniel in the Junius manuscript.
literary_significance: Together with Daniel it shows how Old English poets rendered the canticles of the liturgy in the native heroic idiom, turning scriptural praise into alliterative poetry.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The relationship with Daniel (shared lines) is a standing crux of Old English scholarship; the two poems may derive from a common source or one from the other.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 53r-55v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Lord's Prayer I, II, and III
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (versions I and II); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (version III)
description: Three independent Old English versifications of the Lord's Prayer. The first (123 lines with its doxology) expands each petition into doctrinal and devotional verse; the second (19 lines) is a close rendering; the third, in a Mercian dialect, survives in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
plot_or_argument: Each poem paraphrases the petitions of the Pater Noster — the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil — expanding them with commentary on the soul's needs, the devil's snares, and the last judgment.
narrative_structure: The first version works petition by petition through the prayer, ending with an elaborated doxology; the shorter versions render the prayer more directly with brief homiletic expansions.
literary_form: religious lyric (prayer paraphrase) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the first version's expansions use formulaic homiletic diction familiar from the Exeter Book religious poems.
historical_context: The Lord's Prayer was among the first texts every Christian learned, and Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care singles out prayer as a duty of the learned; vernacular versifications made the prayer available for devotion and meditation in the native idiom.
literary_significance: The fullest surviving Old English treatment of the central Christian prayer, showing how poets turned liturgical texts into vernacular verse of considerable doctrinal ambition.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The three versions are independent texts by different poets, grouped here for convenience as in the standard editions.
bibliographical_notes: Versions I and II in the Exeter Book, first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); version III in CCCC 201; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: Gloria I and II
alternative_titles: The Greater and Lesser Doxology Poems
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: Two short Old English versifications of the liturgical Gloria: Gloria I (57 lines) paraphrases the Greater Doxology sung at Mass, praising the Trinity and Christ the Lamb of God; Gloria II (20 lines) is a brief rendering of the doxology of praise to Father, Son, and Spirit.
plot_or_argument: Gloria I moves from the angels' song of praise through the attributes of the persons of the Trinity to Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, ending with a prayer for mercy. Gloria II offers a compact doxology in verse.
narrative_structure: Both poems are direct liturgical paraphrases; Gloria I is organized by the successive clauses of the Gloria in excelsis, closing with the Agnus Dei petitions.
literary_form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with the balanced parallelism appropriate to liturgical praise; the shorter poem is notably compact.
historical_context: The Benedictine Reform's devotion to the liturgy gave new prominence to the sung ordinary of the Mass; vernacular paraphrases like these made its texts accessible to those whose Latin was limited.
literary_significance: Evidence of the Old English church's project of rendering the central texts of the liturgy into the vernacular poetic idiom.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The two poems are separate compositions.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 125v-127r; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Creed
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A versification of the Apostles' Creed in 57 lines, expanding each article of the faith — the creation, the Incarnation, the Passion, the harrowing of hell, the Ascension, and the last judgment — into alliterative verse of notable doctrinal clarity.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the articles of the Creed in order: God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth; Christ's conception, birth, suffering, death, descent into hell, resurrection, and ascension; and the coming judgment of the living and the dead.
narrative_structure: A sequential paraphrase of the Creed's articles, each expanded with traditional doctrinal imagery (the descent into hell, the trumpet of judgment).
literary_form: religious lyric (creedal paraphrase) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the poem's compact clauses follow the Creed article by article.
historical_context: The Creed was taught to all Christians as the summary of the faith and recited in the daily offices; its versification belongs to the same vernacular devotional project as the Lord's Prayer poems.
literary_significance: The only surviving Old English verse rendering of the Apostles' Creed, valuable for its formulation of Christology and eschatology in the native idiom.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fol. 122; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Kentish Hymn
manuscript_date: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi, fol. 69 (tenth century)
description: A 43-line paraphrase of the Gloria in excelsis in the Kentish dialect, the only substantial Old English poem preserved in that dialect. It praises the Trinity, Christ the Lamb, and the Holy Spirit, and prays for the mercy of the Lord.
plot_or_argument: The poem renders the Greater Doxology clause by clause: praise of God the Father, the Lamb of God who takes away sin, the Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and a closing petition for the Lord's mercy and protection.
narrative_structure: A direct liturgical paraphrase following the order of the Gloria; the doxological clauses are expanded with brief devotional glosses.
literary_form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the Kentish forms of the text are among the few dialectally marked verse survivals outside West Saxon.
historical_context: The hymn was added to a manuscript otherwise containing Kentish glosses and documents; it attests the spread of vernacular liturgical paraphrase beyond the West Saxon heartland of the literary standard.
literary_significance: A rare dialectal witness to Old English religious verse and an early example of the Gloria rendered in English verse.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Cotton Vespasian D.vi; first printed in the nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: Alms-Giving
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A nine-line homiletic poem urging the giving of alms while one still lives, since after death no gift can avail the soul. It is the briefest complete poem in the Exeter Book.
plot_or_argument: The poet exhorts his audience to clothe the naked and feed the hungry now, in life, because the opportunity ends at death, when the soul must face judgment with only what it has given away.
narrative_structure: A single compact exhortation built on the antithesis between the living body's power to give and the corpse's helplessness.
meter_and_prosody: Nine alliterative long lines; compressed formulaic phrasing typical of the Exeter gnomic-homiletic manner.
historical_context: Almsgiving was a central obligation of Anglo-Saxon Christianity, legislated in the law codes and urged in the homilies of Ælfric and Wulfstan; the poem distils that teaching into a single memorable exhortation.
literary_significance: A miniature of the Old English homiletic tradition in verse, showing the poets' capacity for lapidary moral statement.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fol. 121v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: Pharaoh
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: An eight-line fragment on the drowning of Pharaoh's host in the Red Sea, dramatizing the moment when the returning waters destroy the pursuing Egyptians. Probably a fragment of a longer Exodus poem or a brief independent composition.
plot_or_argument: Pharaoh's army, pursuing the Israelites across the sea-bed, is engulfed when the waters return; the poem emphasizes the totality of the destruction and the might of the God who saved his people.
narrative_structure: A single dramatic scene in eight lines, culminating in the overwhelming of the Egyptian host.
literary_form: religious narrative fragment in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Eight alliterative long lines of heroic density; the diction of battle and the sea is that of the heroic tradition applied to scriptural warfare.
historical_context: The Exodus was the type of baptism and of the Church's deliverance throughout Anglo-Saxon literature, most elaborately in the Junius manuscript Exodus.
literary_significance: A witness to the popularity of the Exodus story in Old English verse beyond the Junius manuscript, and to the heroic idiom's capacity to render scriptural battle scenes.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The fragment's relationship to the Junius Exodus is uncertain.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fol. 122r; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Gifts of Men
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
plot_or_argument: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
narrative_structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
literary_significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 78r-80r; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: Precepts
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which a wise father addresses ten counsels to his son, one by one: to avoid anger and envy, choose wise companions, keep faith, practise generosity, and fear God. Each counsel is introduced by a repeated formula of address.
plot_or_argument: The father, speaking 'many winters' of experience, delivers ten distinct precepts to his son on the conduct of a good life — on anger, friendship, wisdom, speech, generosity, and the fear of the Lord — closing with an exhortation to remember the counsels always.
narrative_structure: A decalogue structure: ten formally parallel counsels, each marked by the repeated address 'the wise father said to his son', framed by an introduction and a concluding admonition.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition; the anaphoric frame gives the poem its ceremonial regularity.
historical_context: The father-son instruction poem has biblical and classical roots (Proverbs, the Disticha Catonis) and was a recognized genre in Anglo-Saxon England, as the Old English translation of the Distichs shows.
literary_significance: The most elaborate surviving Old English example of the father-to-son instruction genre, valuable for its picture of the ethical ideals taught to the young Anglo-Saxon elite.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 80r-81r; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: Vainglory
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A moralizing poem of 84 lines contrasting the boastful man, puffed up with wine and pride in the hall, with the wise man who walks humbly before God. The poem analyses the psychology of vainglory and warns that pride corrupts the soul and courts the devil.
plot_or_argument: The poet describes the vainglorious man at the feast, eloquent in self-praise but hollow within, deceived by the devil's arrows of pride; against him is set the wise man of measured speech and right counsel, whom God rewards. The poem closes with the warning that the proud man's fall is certain.
narrative_structure: A diptych structure: parallel portraits of the proud man and the wise man, developed through antithesis, followed by a homiletic conclusion on the wages of pride.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with the homiletic diction of the Exeter religious poems; the hall setting is evoked in the heroic vocabulary of feasting and treasure.
historical_context: Pride was the sin of the heroic hall culture, and the poem turns the imagery of the feast and the boast against its own social setting, in the manner of the homilists' attacks on drunkenness and vainglory.
literary_significance: A penetrating psychological study of pride that fuses the wisdom and homiletic traditions, and a vivid picture of the moral dangers of the Anglo-Saxon feast-hall.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, fols. 84v-85v; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Order of the World
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
description: A wisdom poem of some 102 lines in which the poet urges his hearer to contemplate the created order — the sun's course, the stars, the seasons, and the harmony of the world — and to praise the Creator who sustains it all. The poem is an exercise in natural contemplation leading to worship.
plot_or_argument: The poet calls on his audience to observe the wonders of creation: the journey of the sun, the movement of the heavens, the alternation of day and night, the order of the seasons. From the beauty and regularity of the world he turns to its maker, whom all creation serves, and urges man to praise God while he lives.
narrative_structure: An exhortation framed as direct address to a 'wise one', moving from the observation of nature through reflection on the Creator to a closing call to praise; the poem is built of successive contemplations of the cosmic order.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; the descriptive passages on the heavens and seasons use the formulaic resources of the wisdom tradition with unusual lyrical polish.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom corpus and shares its cosmological interests with the metrical version of Psalm 18 and the creation passages of the Cædmonian poems; it reflects the monastic ideal of contemplating God through his works.
literary_significance: One of the finest Old English poems of natural contemplation, notable for its integration of cosmology and devotion.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book; first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); standard edition in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936).

title: The Judgement Day I and II
manuscript_date: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (Judgement Day I); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (Judgement Day II)
description: Two independent eschatological poems on the last judgment. Judgement Day I (119 lines) describes the cosmic terrors of doomsday and the soul's reckoning; Judgement Day II (306 lines), based on Bede's De die iudicii, is a sustained meditation on sin, penance, and the judgment, addressed to the individual soul.
plot_or_argument: Judgement Day I depicts the universal conflagration, the trumpets, and the assembly of all souls before the judge, contrasting the fate of the blessed and the damned. Judgement Day II urges the penitent soul to recall its sins now, while confession is still possible, painting the terrors of judgment in images of fire, darkness, and weeping, and closes with hope for those who repent.
narrative_structure: Both poems move from description of the cosmic catastrophe to exhortation; Judgement Day II is organized as a sequence of meditations on sin, the hour of death, the judgment, and the possibility of mercy through penance.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; Judgement Day II's sustained length and homiletic urgency make it the most ambitious of the Exeter/CCCC 201 eschatological poems.
historical_context: The judgment was the master-image of Anglo-Saxon homiletics, from the Blickling and Vercelli homilies to Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi; the poems belong to that culture of penitential fear and are the verse counterpart of the homilists' doomsday rhetoric.
literary_significance: The fullest Old English verse treatments of the last judgment, and (in Judgement Day II) an important vernacular witness to the reception of Bede's Latin eschatological poetry.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The two poems are independent compositions; Judgement Day II is an adaptation of Bede's De die iudicii, not by Bede himself.
bibliographical_notes: Judgement Day I in the Exeter Book, first printed in Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis (1842); Judgement Day II in CCCC 201; standard editions in Krapp and Dobbie, ASPR III (1936) and Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: An Exhortation to Christian Living
manuscript_date: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
description: A homiletic poem of ninety-two lines urging its audience to keep God's commandments, resist the devil, and live in readiness for death and judgment. The poem is direct, urgent, and practical in its moral teaching.
plot_or_argument: The poet exhorts the faithful to love God, keep his commands, avoid sin and the devil's snares, and remember the brevity of life and the certainty of judgment; wealth and pleasure are fleeting, but the soul's fate is eternal.
narrative_structure: A sequence of direct exhortations in the second person, each grounded in the antithesis between this world's brevity and the soul's eternity, closing with the promise of heavenly reward.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with the homiletic formulas of late Old English preaching; the verse is plain and expository rather than ornamental.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the late Old English group of CCCC 201 (with Judgement Day II, A Summons to Prayer, and the Menologium), texts associated with the Benedictine Reform's devotional and catechetical programme.
literary_significance: A representative of the reform movement's verse catechesis, showing the homiletic mode of late Old English poetry at its most direct.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: CCCC 201; first printed in the nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: A Summons to Prayer
manuscript_date: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
description: A short poem calling the faithful to prayer at the ringing of the church bell, celebrating the power of the Lord's Prayer to guard the soul and summoning all creation to join in worship.
plot_or_argument: At the sound of the bell the poet summons the congregation to prayer: the Lord's Prayer is a shield against the devil, and prayer joins earth to heaven; the poem closes by calling on all beings to praise the Lord.
narrative_structure: A liturgical summons organized around the bell, the prayer, and the assembly of creation in praise.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line, brief and incantatory, suited to its liturgical occasion.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the CCCC 201 group and reflects the Benedictine Reform's emphasis on the daily offices and the sanctification of time through prayer.
literary_significance: A rare Old English poem tied to the actual practice of the daily office, and a small masterpiece of liturgical verse.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: CCCC 201; first printed in the nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: The Menologium
manuscript_date: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.i (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201), eleventh century
description: A metrical calendar of the church year in 231 lines, versifying the fixed feasts and saints' days from Christmas through the year to Advent, with careful attention to the intervals of days between festivals. It is prefixed to the C-text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
plot_or_argument: The poem proceeds through the liturgical year — Christmas, Epiphany, the spring feasts, Easter's movable cycle, the summer and autumn saints' days, and the return of Advent — computing the days between the major festivals and naming the saints honoured in the English church.
narrative_structure: A strictly sequential calendar, each feast introduced with its date and interval from the last; the structure is numerical and liturgical rather than narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line disciplined to the calendar's enumerative demands; the poet's art lies in varying formulaic phrasing within a rigid frame.
historical_context: The poem reflects the English church's calendar as reformed in the tenth century, and its position beside the Chronicle shows the integration of liturgical and historical time in Benedictine Reform culture.
literary_significance: The only surviving Old English metrical calendar, and a document of the English church's festal year at the height of the Benedictine Reform.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: CCCC 201 (Cotton Tiberius B.i); first printed in the nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: Homiletic Fragment I and II
manuscript_date: Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), late tenth century
description: Two homiletic poems in the Vercelli Book. Homiletic Fragment I (47 lines) is a meditation on deceitful friendship, comparing the false friend to the bee whose honey is sweet but whose sting is deadly. Homiletic Fragment II (20 lines) laments man's hardness of heart amid the world's sorrows.
plot_or_argument: Fragment I warns against the friend who speaks fair but plots evil, elaborating the image of the bee through biblical and proverbial wisdom. Fragment II meditates on grief and the human failure to heed the truth, in a fragmentary surviving text.
narrative_structure: Fragment I develops a single governing simile (the treacherous friend as bee) with proverbial expansions; Fragment II is a broken meditation on sorrow and heedlessness.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line in the homiletic manner of the Vercelli Book's prose sermons; both texts are imperfectly preserved.
historical_context: The Vercelli Book pairs these poems with its collection of doomsday homilies and with The Dream of the Rood, Elene, and Andreas; the fragments belong to the same culture of vernacular preaching and moral verse.
literary_significance: Witnesses to the close relationship between Old English homiletic prose and verse, and to the moral psychology of the late Anglo-Saxon church.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The two fragments are distinct poems.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, fols. 104r-106r; first printed in Blume's Iter Italicum (1836); standard edition in Krapp, ASPR II (1932).

title: The Rune Poem
manuscript_date: London, British Library, Cotton Otho B.x, fol. 165 (destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731; survives in the transcript printed by George Hickes, 1705)
description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which each of the 29 runes of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc is given a stanza beginning with the rune's name and elaborating its traditional meanings: feoh (wealth), ur (aurochs), thorn, the gods, the horse, the sun, and the rest. The poem fuses native Germanic rune-lore with Christian wisdom.
plot_or_argument: Stanza by stanza, the poem unfolds the lore of each rune — wealth's mutability, the aurochs' ferocity, thorn's sharpness, the sun's blessing to seafarers, the grave's coldness — building a gnomic encyclopaedia of the natural and social world as encoded in the runic alphabet.
narrative_structure: A catalogue of 29 stanzas, one per rune, in the fixed order of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc; each stanza is a self-contained gnomic meditation introduced by the rune-name.
literary_form: runic wisdom poem in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line; each stanza opens with the rune's name, and the verses carry the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition.
historical_context: The poem is the fullest surviving statement of the Anglo-Saxon runic tradition, composed when runes were still written for inscriptions and magic while the script's pagan associations were being absorbed into Christian learning; it descends from the same tradition as the Old Norwegian and Old Icelandic rune poems.
literary_significance: The principal source for the names and meanings of the Anglo-Saxon runes, and a bridge between Germanic pagan lore and Christian Old English poetry; its loss in the 1731 fire makes Hickes's transcript the only witness.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The prose and verse traditions around the runes descend from a common Germanic inheritance; the Old English poem is an independent composition.
bibliographical_notes: Cotton Otho B.x; printed by George Hickes in the Linguarum veterum septentrionalium thesaurus (1705); standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942), and Halsall's critical edition (1981).

title: Seasons for Fasting
manuscript_date: London, British Library, Additional MS 43703 (a sixteenth-century transcript by Laurence Nowell of the lost Cotton Otho B.xi)
description: A poem of some 230 lines on the proper observance of the Ember fasts, defending the English custom of four seasonal fasts against the laxity of those who fast only once a year, and citing biblical and canonical authority for the practice. The text breaks off imperfectly.
plot_or_argument: The poet rebukes priests who observe the Ember days wrongly, argues from scripture (Moses, Elijah, the Ninevites, Christ's forty days) that fasting is commanded, sets out the correct times of the four seasonal fasts, and attacks drunken priests; the poem ends incomplete amid a catalogue of fasts.
narrative_structure: An argumentative structure: rebuke, biblical proof-texts, prescription of the fasts, and invective against clerical abuses, in the manner of Wulfstanian homiletic verse.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long line with the homiletic urgency of Wulfstan's prose; the text is incomplete, and some lines are metrically irregular.
historical_context: The poem belongs to the late Old English period's debates over ecclesiastical discipline, contemporary with Wulfstan's legislation on fasting and the reform of the clergy; its strictures on drunken priests echo the reformers' campaigns.
literary_significance: A rare Old English poem on a live question of ecclesiastical discipline, valuable for its picture of eleventh-century religious controversy and its fusion of homiletic and satirical verse.
attribution_notes: Anonymous. The poem's Wulfstanian manner has suggested to some scholars an origin in his circle, but no attribution is established.
bibliographical_notes: Nowell's transcript, BL Add. 43703; first printed in the late nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942).

title: Bede's Death Song
manuscript_date: St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek 254 (ninth century or earlier); Northumbrian version in Cambridge, University Library Kk.5.16 (the Moore Bede, c. 737)
description: A five-line alliterative poem, the last words of the dying Bede, recorded in the Epistola Cuthberti de obitu Bedae. The poet meditates on the soul's necessary journey out of the body and the judgment each man must face for his deeds. It is the earliest datable Old English poem.
plot_or_argument: Bede, near death, reflects that no man's wisdom can outrun his need to consider, before departing, what judgment his soul will receive for the good and evil he has done.
narrative_structure: Five alliterative long lines in two movements: the inevitability of the soul's departure, and the reckoning of deeds before the judge.
meter_and_prosody: Five lines of classic alliterative verse in the Northumbrian dialect, preserved with Latin paraphrase; the earliest securely datable example of English poetry.
historical_context: Recorded by Bede's pupil Cuthbert in the letter describing the master's death on 26 May 735; the poem circulated in two dialect versions and in many manuscripts of the Historia ecclesiastica, often with a Latin translation.
literary_significance: The earliest datable poem in English, and a uniquely documented case of vernacular verse preserved with its author, date, and occasion of composition.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Bede in the Epistola Cuthberti, composed, according to the letter, on his deathbed; the attribution is accepted by modern scholarship, though the poem circulated anonymously in some manuscripts.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942); printed in the nineteenth century and in all modern collections of the minor poems.

title: The Leiden Riddle
manuscript_date: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Lat. Q. 106, fol. 25v (c. 800, Northumbrian)
description: A fourteen-line Old English riddle translating Aldhelm's Latin Enigma 33 on the mail-coat (lorica): the garment made of many small iron rings, woven by no woman's hands, that guards the warrior's breast. It is the earliest surviving English riddle, preserved in a Northumbrian dialect.
plot_or_argument: The riddle-speaker describes itself: a garment whose countless rings are joined without thread, forged of iron by smiths' skill, protecting the breast of the warrior who wears it in battle. The solution is the mail-coat (lorica).
narrative_structure: A classic first-person riddle in the Aldhelmian manner, moving from the material of the object to its making to its use in war.
meter_and_prosody: Fourteen alliterative long lines translating Aldhelm's hexameters; the poem keeps the riddle's obliquity while adapting it to vernacular alliterative technique.
historical_context: Written into the last leaf of a Leiden manuscript of the Latin riddles, the poem documents the translation of Aldhelmian learning into Northumbrian vernacular verse in the age of Bede; it is the direct ancestor of the Exeter Book riddle tradition.
literary_significance: The earliest surviving English riddle and the earliest evidence of the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition's translation into the vernacular, bridging Aldhelm and the Exeter Book.
attribution_notes: Anonymous translation of Aldhelm's Enigma 33 ('Lorica'); the translator is unknown.
bibliographical_notes: Leiden, Voss. Lat. Q. 106; printed in the nineteenth century; standard edition in Dobbie, ASPR VI (1942); see also Smith, Three Northumbrian Poems (1933).
